title: Control Plane Risk Framing and Sales Proposal Notes
body:
Purpose and audience: quick reference for sales and solutions engineering when responding to regulated buyers who ask about the private control plane model, data residency, and contractual guarantees. This is a working sketch: use snippets in proposals and adapt to buyer-specific terminology.

Executive positioning (one-liner): Redwood Private provides a customer-isolated control plane that gives your legal, security, and platform teams the observability, key control points, and contractual commitments they need to run regulated AI workloads — without forcing you to build and operate an inference stack from scratch.

Key messages to lead with (short):
- Ownership boundary: customer owns data and networking; Redwood operates a thin control plane that coordinates model lifecycle and telemetry but has no access to plaintext customer inputs/outputs when KMS and network controls are enforced.
- Observable and auditable: full audit trail for rollout events, model changes, and operator actions with exportable logs and retention controls mapped to customer policy.
- Contractable controls: encryption-at-rest/in-transit, KMS/HSM integration, private peering, SOC2/ISO references, and SLAs that map to tiered availability and incident response commitments.

Common buyer concerns and rebuttals (short scripts):
- Concern: "Will Redwood have access to our PII inside requests?"
  - Rebuttal: "By default no. For VPC private control planes we integrate your KMS and network ACLs to ensure that decryption keys and control-plane APIs are behind your network boundary. We can include contractual language about data access, and provide demo of end-to-end flow where logs in the control plane are redacted unless customer issues an explicit enable request, logged and auditable."
- Concern: "Is the control plane a central attack surface?"
  - Rebuttal: "We treat the control plane as a minimal orchestrator: it never stores plaintext inference payloads in production when the private option is enabled. It uses signed manifests and versioned model artifacts; all sensitive operations require mutually authenticated mTLS and are logged. We can provide architecture diagrams, pen-test reports, and a hybrid runbook showing our containment procedures for suspicious operator activity."
- Concern: "How does Redwood handle incident response and forensics for Private customers?"
  - Rebuttal: "We propose a joint runbook: customer-led triage within their network boundary augmented by Redwood remote-support sessions per contract. For higher tiers, we include 24x7 on-call and forensic-readout deliverables within defined SLAs."

Competitive framing (short comparative points):
- Against cloud AI endpoints: Cloud providers give managed GPUs but often lack a consistent auditable control plane tailored to model rollouts and prompt-level tracing. Redwood provides per-deployment rollout controls, canarying, and model rollback semantics tied to audit trails.
- Against LLM API vendors: Many providers operate a shared multitenant control plane; they may not allow KMS/HSM integrations or fine-grained network isolation. Redwood Private is designed to meet procurement/legal gating for regulated verticals.
- Against self-hosted runtimes: Building in-house buys you control but costs months of engineering and ongoing SRE ops. Redwood offers a prescriptive control plane with hardened operational practices and integration points (SSO, KMS, SIEM) so customers get control without building the orchestration and observability layers themselves.

Proposal-level negotiation levers (for AE & PS):
- Pricing: charge for control plane subscription + reserved capacity. Offer a ramp (90 days pilot at reduced control plane fee) and commit discounts for multi-year reserved capacity.
- SLAs: tiered availability (bronze/silver/gold) with credits and a separate incident notification SLA. Buyers in regulated industries frequently require an escalation SLA and quarterly compliance reviews — price those into an enterprise add-on.
- Runbook and on-call: include a standard runbook in the SOW; higher-tier customers can get named engineers and war-room support at extra cost.

Sample legal/contract asks to pre-empt:
- Add clause: Redwood will not access customer plaintext inference payloads unless explicitly authorized by the customer or by court order; procedures for emergency access must require multi-party signoff and auditability.
- Add clause: data deletion/retention windows for artifacts, and proof-of-deletion process for model snapshots and cached KV.
- Add clause: right to audit / periodic SOC2/ISO attestations and provide pen test summaries under NDA.

Technical appendix (language for SEs):
- Control plane flow (textual): customer control plane sits inside customer VPC. Redwood control-plane agents are deployed into a management subnet (customer-managed or Redwood-hosted on dedicated infra per agreement). Communication is mTLS with mutual auth; keys kept in customer KMS. Model artifacts are pulled into the customer deployment via signed manifests; inference happens inside the customer's private network. Telemetry is optionally shuttled to Redwood observability endpoints via an encrypted, one-way push that can be configured to filter or redact inputs.
- Identity & keys: SSO via SAML/OIDC for operator roles; RBAC mapped to LDAP/IdP groups; KMS integration must allow Redwood controllers to obtain ephemeral decryption tokens; for HSM customers we support PKCS#11 binding.
- Audit & logs: Offer streams (syslog/CloudWatch/Event Hubs) and flat-file SNAs. Provide log schemas for operator events, rollout events, model versioning, and API calls. Include guidance for retention and export.

Proof-of-concept (PoC) checklist and success criteria (for AE & SE):
- Setup: network peering established, KMS keys provisioned, SSO test user created, minimal control plane agent deployed.
- Test cases: model rollout canary works; rollback triggers; encrypted model artifact fetch; logs show operator action; inference payloads processed within customer subnet and not visible via Redwood-hosted consoles.
- Success criteria: (< 2 business days) to stand up a functional PoC; demonstrable audit trail for 3 operator actions; one successful canary rollback.

Sales enablement snippets (one-liners for calls):
- "We don't need to see your data to serve your models — you control the keys and the network boundary."
- "Our control plane gives your compliance team an auditable policy layer for rollouts and operator activity without handing over data ownership."

Open questions / risks we should resolve before next pilot batch: list of product decisions and asks for engineering and legal.
- Can we standardize a minimal HSM integration pattern for PoCs so SEs can demo within 48 hours?
- What level of redaction tooling do we ship by default for telemetry? (Engineering input needed on UX and cost.)
- Legal: prepared language for emergency access and proof-of-deletion; confirm with privacy counsel what we can commit in standard SOW.

Action items (owners):
- SE kit: Marco — produce a one-page architecture diagram and a short recorded demo of PoC flow.
- Legal draft: Leah — produce a recommended emergency-access clause and deletion playbook for SOWs.
- Product: Aisha — prioritize a small UX change to enable telemetry redaction toggles in the console for Private deployments (MVP scope).

Notes to reuse when drafting proposals: keep language concrete, focus on observable controls (logs, RBAC, KMS), and always map technical controls to buyer-level risks (data exposure, auditability, uptime). Use the PoC checklist to reduce procurement friction — buyers can sign for a 30–90 day pilot with narrow success criteria and an explicit fallback path to terminate.

End of note.
